suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Async legacy writes are tied to the request context, which is canceled as soon as the HTTP request completes, so the background legacy write is silently aborted with context.Canceled.
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: The async legacy writes in Create (dualwriter_mode3.go:50-57), Delete (108-114), Update (134-141) and DeleteCollection (161-167) derive their context from the request-scoped ctx via context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...), and that request context is canceled as soon as the HTTP request completes. WHY: The legacy write is SQL-bound (e.g., playlist legacy Create inserts via s.service.Create, legacy_storage.go:115), so any legacy write that outlives the response window — most bulk DeleteCollections, or any write under DB latency — is aborted with context.Canceled, silently (the goroutine only records a metric), which defeats mode 3's purpose of writing to legacy as a safe measure and permanently diverges the two stores since mode 3 has no reconciliation. HOW: Detach from the request before spawning, e.g. `go func() { ctx := context.WithoutCancel(ctx); ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, time.Second*10, ...); ... }()` in all four goroutines, and consider logging the legacy error inside the goroutine since it is currently invisible.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Storage failure paths in Create/Update record the legacy metric (and never record the storage metric), the DeleteCollection goroutine records the legacy op under the storage metric, and Delete's success path uses the object name as the kind label.
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: Metric recorder call-sites are swapped at three places in the new code: Create's storage-error path (dualwriter_mode3.go:45) and Update's storage-error path (line 129) call `recordLegacyDuration(...)` for a failure in the unified Storage, and DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine (line 166) calls `recordStorageDuration(...)` for the LegacyStorage operation; additionally Delete's success path (line 106) passes `name` where the `kind` label is expected (its own error path at line 103 uses options.Kind). WHY: `recordLegacyDuration`/`recordStorageDuration` observe different Prometheus histograms (`grafana_dual_writer_legacy_duration_seconds` vs `grafana_dual_writer_storage_duration_seconds`, metrics.go:54-62), so storage create/update failures show up as phantom legacy errors, storage failures are never visible in the storage metric, and legacy delete-collection activity is credited to storage — corrupting the migration dashboards/alerts used to decide when it is safe to move off legacy. HOW: Use `recordStorageDuration(true, ...)` on the error paths at lines 45 and 129, `recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, ...)` inside the DeleteCollection goroutine at line 166, and `options.Kind` (not `name`) at line 106, matching the mode 2 implementation (dualwriter_mode2.go:48/61/151/200-203).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Legacy Update no longer receives the object that unified storage wrote (the updateWrapper was dropped), so legacy recomputes the update from its own old object and can silently persist a different result — or fail NotFound and never write at all.
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: Update's async legacy write (dualwriter_mode3.go:139) passes the raw `objInfo` to d.Legacy.Update instead of wrapping it with `updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: res}` as the previous implementation did, so legacy recomputes `objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, oldFromLegacy)` against its own old object rather than persisting the object the unified store wrote. WHY: The playlist legacy storage's Update does Get-then-apply (legacy_storage.go:142-145) — if the legacy row is missing it returns NotFound (silently swallowed by the goroutine, so the row is never created in legacy), and if it is stale the recomputed object differs from what storage wrote (e.g., for PATCH-based objInfo); combined with fire-and-forget goroutines that can apply concurrent updates out of order, legacy silently and permanently diverges, which is exactly what the dual-write "safe measure" is supposed to prevent. HOW: Keep mirroring the storage result: capture `res` after the storage Update succeeds and pass `&updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: res}` to d.Legacy.Update (updateWrapper is still defined in dualwriter.go:128-140).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Delete now early-returns on any storage error — including NotFound — so objects that exist only in legacy storage are never deleted from legacy, a cleanup the previous implementation deliberately performed.
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: Delete (dualwriter_mode3.go:101-105) returns early on every storage error — including NotFound — so the legacy delete goroutine (lines 108-114) never runs when the object is absent from unified storage but still present in legacy storage. WHY: The previous implementation deliberately tolerated storage NotFound (`if !apierrors.IsNotFound(err)` before returning) and still performed the legacy delete; rows that exist only in legacy are realistic (objects created under mode 0-2 before the org moved to mode 3, or any legacy row whose unified counterpart was never written), and with the early return those rows can never be cleaned through the API — they are invisible (mode 3 reads storage-only) yet permanently orphaned in the SQL database, breaking the rollback/cleanup story the dual-write exists to protect. HOW: On storage NotFound, still spawn the legacy delete goroutine (optionally skipping it only for non-NotFound errors), e.g. `if err != nil && !apierrors.IsNotFound(err) { return res, async, err }` before the goroutine block, and return the storage error to the caller as before.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Delete stores the base d.Log into the context instead of the enriched `log`, losing the name/kind/method fields for all downstream logging in both the storage and async legacy delete calls.
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: Delete builds the enriched logger `log` (dualwriter_mode3.go:96) but then stores the base `d.Log` into the context: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` (line 97) instead of `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)`. WHY: Both d.Storage.Delete (line 100) and the async legacy delete goroutine (line 110) receive a context whose logger lacks the name/kind/method values, so any storage implementation that reads the logger via klog.FromContext loses the request correlation that every other method in this file (Create:39, Get:66, List:82, Update:123, DeleteCollection:150) deliberately provides. HOW: Change line 97 to `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, log)` to match the other five methods.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: No mode-3 test asserts that the asynchronous legacy write actually happens — deleting the legacy-write goroutine entirely would still pass every unit and integration test.
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: The new mode-3 unit tests (TestMode3_Create dualwriter_mode3_test.go:47-77, and the Delete/Update/DeleteCollection equivalents) never assert that the legacy write actually happens — the replaced (commented-out) test asserted `lsSpy.Counts("LegacyStorage.Create") == 1`, but the new tests only check the unified-store result because the legacy call now runs in a fire-and-forget goroutine that races with subtest completion. WHY: Mode 3's defining feature is the background write to legacy; with no assertion on the legacy mock (and integration tests that read only from unified storage), removing the `go func()` blocks in dualwriter_mode3.go:50/108/134/161 or silently failing every legacy write would still pass the entire suite — a critical test gap for the exact behavior this PR introduces. HOW: Make the async write observable and deterministic before asserting: e.g. have the mock signal a channel (or use mock.WaitUntil/AssertNumberOfCalls with a small wait) and assert `LegacyStorage.Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection` was invoked once for each write-path success case.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Delete success path passes `name` where `options.Kind` belongs in the kind label of the storage-duration metric.
suggestions.suggestionContent: On Delete's success path, `recordStorageDuration` receives `name` in the third (kind) argument position. Every sibling call in this file — Delete's own error path (line 103: `recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, ...)`) and its legacy goroutine (line 113: `recordLegacyDuration(..., options.Kind, ...)`), plus Create/Get/List/Update/DeleteCollection — passes `options.Kind` there. Result: every successful delete is labeled kind=<object name>, breaking per-kind latency/error aggregation and creating one metric label value per object name (unbounded cardinality).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine records the legacy duration via recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The DeleteCollection legacy goroutine measures the Legacy call (`d.Legacy.DeleteCollection`, line 165, timed from `startLegacy`) but records it with `recordStorageDuration`, whereas the equivalent legacy goroutines in Create (line 56), Delete (line 113) and Update (line 140) all use `recordLegacyDuration`. Legacy delete-collection durations and errors are therefore published under the storage metric, so storage latency/error dashboards include legacy-write measurements.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Create's storage failure is recorded via recordLegacyDuration with the storage start time instead of recordStorageDuration.
suggestions.suggestionContent: Create's storage-error path calls `recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`: a storage failure timed from `startStorage` is written to the legacy metric. The parallel error path in Delete (line 103) correctly uses `recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. Storage write failures are thus counted as legacy-write failures with storage latency, skewing both series.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Update's storage failure is recorded via recordLegacyDuration with the storage start time instead of recordStorageDuration.
suggestions.suggestionContent: Update's storage-error path mirrors Create's mistake: it calls `recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`, recording the storage update failure/latency under the legacy metric, while Delete's error path (line 103) shows the intended pattern `recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Mode3's fire-and-forget legacy writes run on the request-scoped context that is canceled when the handler returns, contradicting the dual-write contract that this PR's own playlist integration subtests (and the retained doc comment) depend on.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The legacy half of Mode3 dual-write now runs in a goroutine that derives its context from the request-scoped `ctx` (`context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` at lines 51, 110, 135, 163). The handler returns immediately after the Storage write, and net/http cancels the request context as soon as the HTTP handler finishes — so the goroutine's child context is born canceled and `d.Legacy.Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection` aborts with "context canceled", silently dropping the legacy copy. This breaks the contract that the other changed files in this PR assume: dualwriter_mode3.go:23/:35 still documents Mode3 as "writing to LegacyStorage and Storage", and the new playlist_test.go subtests ("with dual write (file, mode 3)" / "with dual write (unified storage, mode 3)", lines 132-144 and 191-204) set `grafanarest.Mode3` with the comment "Required so that legacy calls are also written" — they will flake or silently under-verify because the legacy write races request-context cancellation. The new unit tests in dualwriter_mode3_test.go never catch this because they pass `context.Background()` (never canceled), upholding a premise the real request path violates. Fix: decouple the background write from request cancellation, e.g. `ctx := context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` before deriving the 10s timeout (and keep the request's logging values), or perform the legacy write synchronously before returning — and make the tests await the legacy call so both test hunks encode the same assumption.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The rewritten mode-3 tests only assert the storage half of the dual write, so removing the legacy write entirely would leave every TestMode3_* test green.
suggestions.suggestionContent: None of the TestMode3_* tests verify the legacy half of the dual write. Mode 3's defining behavior is 'write to LegacyStorage and Storage' (dualwriter_mode3.go:50–57, 108–114, 134–141, 161–167), but every test asserts only the object returned by the synchronous Storage call and returns immediately; the legacy write happens in a fire-and-forget goroutine that the test never waits for, and m.AssertExpectations is never called, so the legacy mock expectations are never checked. Delete the four `go func(){ d.Legacy.… }` blocks from dualwriter_mode3.go and every test in this file still passes. Give the tests teeth: use separate mocks per backend (see next suggestion), and after the synchronous call, wait for the async legacy write and assert it was invoked (e.g., require.Eventually on mock call counts, or expose a synchronization hook / make the legacy write synchronous under test).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Legacy and storage mocks share one *mock.Mock, so the tests cannot tell which backend was called — the storage call in the 'storage fails' case is actually served by the legacy-set expectation.
suggestions.suggestionContent: Every subtest builds legacyStoreMock{m, l} and storageMock{m, s} over the SAME *mock.Mock (lines 49–54 and the identical blocks in Get/List/Delete/DeleteCollection/Update), so both backends match the same m.On("Create"/"Delete"/…) expectations and the tests cannot distinguish which backend was invoked or how many times each was called. Proof: the case 'error when creating object in the unified store fails' (lines 37–44) sets no storage expectation at all — d.Storage.Create at dualwriter_mode3.go:42 passes only because it matches the expectation registered under the legacy setup. This neutralizes the dual-write verification the file is named after (the deleted spy-based test counted LegacyStorage.Create and Storage.Create separately). Use one *mock.Mock per backend so legacy and storage expectations are asserted independently.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The new 'with dual write (…, mode 3)' playlist subtests read only from unified storage, so they would still pass if the async legacy write never happened.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The new subtests named "with dual write (file/unified/etcd, mode 3)" configure Mode3 but cannot observe the dual-write behavior they are named after: in mode 3, DualWriterMode3.Get/List read only from unified Storage (dualwriter_mode3.go:63–92), and the legacy write is a fire-and-forget goroutine (dualwriter_mode3.go:50–57) that the test never waits on — doPlaylistTests' assertions are all served from unified storage, so a broken/silent-failure legacy write leaves these subtests green. To actually cover mode 3's dual-write, after doPlaylistTests (or per-operation) wait for the async legacy write and assert the object exists in the legacy store (e.g., query the legacy SQL/file store with require.Eventually); otherwise these subtests are equivalent to the mode-0/mode-2 runs.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Async legacy writes inherit the request context, which is cancelled as soon as the handler returns, so legacy writes race request teardown and silently fail.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The legacy-write goroutines in Create (50-57), Delete (108-114), Update (134-141) and DeleteCollection (161-167) do `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10s, ...)` where `ctx` is the incoming *request* context. In net/http the request context is cancelled when ServeHTTP returns — i.e. right after Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection return to the apiserver handler. The child timeout context is therefore cancelled almost immediately; the legacy write usually fails with `context canceled`, the error is swallowed (only recorded into a metric), and legacy storage silently diverges from unified storage — the exact invariant mode 3 exists to maintain. Legacy-API readers then see stale/missing objects, and there is no retry. The unit tests never catch this because they pass context.Background(), which is never cancelled. Detach from the request's cancellation before applying the timeout (Go >= 1.21 `context.WithoutCancel`), or keep values but drop cancellation, e.g. build the timeout from a detached context.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Fire-and-forget legacy goroutines allow writes to reach legacy storage out of order, leaving it with an older object version than unified storage.
suggestions.suggestionContent: Because the response is returned (line 116) before the legacy write goroutine (108-114) is guaranteed to have run — and never awaited — a client that sequentially issues Update A, gets its 200, then issues Update A' can have the two legacy goroutines execute in either order. Legacy storage can end with A (older) while unified holds A' (newer). The same hazard exists for a delete followed by a re-create of the same name: the legacy delete may land after the legacy create and remove the new object. Synchronous dual-writes (as in mode 1/2 and the previous implementation) guaranteed legacy was written before the response. Serialize the legacy writes (single worker queue per dual writer or per resource) or keep them synchronous to preserve ordering.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Multiple metric calls record the wrong storage/backend or the wrong label: storage failures recorded as legacy, a legacy op recorded as storage, and the object name passed as the kind label.
suggestions.suggestionContent: Four recording calls corrupt the dual-write metrics that operators rely on to decide when it is safe to migrate modes: (a) line 45 — a *storage* Create failure is recorded via recordLegacyDuration(true, ...), inflating legacy error counts; (b) line 129 — same bug for Update's storage failure; (c) line 166 — the *legacy* DeleteCollection is recorded via recordStorageDuration(...), polluting storage duration histograms with legacy timings; (d) line 106 — Delete's success path passes the object `name` as the kind argument while the sibling error path (line 103) passes `options.Kind`; besides being inconsistent for the same metric series, object names are unbounded user-controlled strings, so they land in a Prometheus label and blow up cardinality. Fix each call to use the correct recorder (recordStorageDuration for storage outcomes, recordLegacyDuration for legacy outcomes) and `options.Kind` consistently.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Update no longer wraps objInfo with updateWrapper, so legacy re-computes the updated object from its own state and can store different content than unified storage committed.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The previous implementation passed `&updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}` to Legacy.Update so both stores committed the exact object unified computed. The new goroutine (line 139) passes the raw `objInfo`, so legacy re-invokes `objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old)` against legacy's own current object. If the two stores are (transiently) diverged — the normal state mode 3 tolerates — a patch-style UpdatedObjectInfo produces a different result for legacy than for unified, making the divergence permanent instead of converging. Also note this runs under the request-cancelled context from the first finding. Restore the updateWrapper (or equivalent) so legacy stores the object unified actually committed.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Async legacy dual-writes reuse the request context, which is canceled the moment the handler returns, so the background legacy write almost always aborts and mode-3 legacy writes silently never happen.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The new fire-and-forget legacy writes derive their context from the request-scoped ctx (context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...) at :51, and the same pattern at :110, :135, :163). The request context is canceled as soon as the REST handler returns and the HTTP response is written, so the background d.Legacy.Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection call races against its parent's cancellation and will typically abort with 'context canceled' — the 10s timeout is moot. Before this PR the legacy write ran synchronously with a live context, so callers (legacy SQL-backed Grafana APIs reading the legacy copy) could rely on mode-3 dual writes actually reaching legacy storage; that contract is now silently broken and legacy writes essentially never land in production. Detach from the request lifecycle: build the timeout from context.WithoutCancel(ctx) (or context.Background()) before launching each goroutine.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Update dropped the updateWrapper for the legacy store, so legacy now recomputes the update against its own stale old object and the two stores can persist divergent objects.
suggestions.suggestionContent: Update no longer passes the storage-computed object to the legacy store. The old implementation computed `updated` once from storage's old object and wrapped it via &updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}, guaranteeing both stores persisted the identical object; mode 2 still does this (dualwriter_mode2.go:298). The new goroutine at :139 calls d.Legacy.Update with the raw objInfo, so legacy re-runs objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, legacyOld) against its own copy — which differs in resourceVersion, timestamps, or content for objects not yet fully mirrored. For patch-style updates the two stores can now persist divergent objects (or legacy fails its RV precondition, or resurrects via forceAllowCreate), losing the 'same object in both stores' guarantee that consumers of the dual-write migration rely on. Restore the updateWrapper for the legacy call (wrapping the object returned by d.Storage.Update at :126).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Delete no longer falls through to the legacy store on unified-storage NotFound, leaving pre-migration legacy-only objects permanently uncleaned.
suggestions.suggestionContent: Delete previously tolerated a NotFound from unified storage (apierrors.IsNotFound) and still proceeded to delete the legacy copy — that path was the only way to clean up objects that exist only in legacy storage (created before mode 3 was enabled for the resource). The new code returns immediately on any storage error at :101-104, before the legacy goroutine at :108 is ever launched, so legacy-only rows become permanently undeletable through the API: the caller gets the same 404 as before but silently loses the legacy-cleanup side effect it used to get. If skipping legacy on storage failure is intentional for non-NotFound errors, at least keep the NotFound case falling through to the legacy delete (or always attempt legacy cleanup, as the old code did).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Init moved into NewResourceServer turns the pre-existing bleve.New 'path already exists' collision into a permanent Grafana boot failure on every restart once any namespace exceeds the 10-doc file threshold.
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: `NewResourceServer` now calls `s.Init(ctx)` during construction and returns `nil, err` on any init failure (server.go:258-262), but the search init it makes fatal re-runs `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` on `<IndexPath>/<namespace>/<resource>.<group>` (bleve.go:96-98), and bleve.New returns `ErrorIndexPathExists` whenever that directory already exists — there is no `bleve.Open` fallback and no cleanup of the index dir anywhere. WHY: with `index_file_threshold` defaulting to 10 and `index_min_count` to 1 (setting_unified_storage.go:44-45), the first boot of any deployment with `FlagUnifiedStorageSearch` enabled and any namespace holding >10 docs of a resource persists a file-based index; on the NEXT restart the in-memory cache is empty, `GetIndex` returns nil, `BuildIndex` errors, `search.init` propagates the error, and now — new in this PR — `NewResourceServer` fails, so the server (sql/service.go:113, client.go:101) cannot start at all; previously the same error only broke search lazily while Grafana booted. The same collision also occurs on FIRST boot when two ResourceServer instances are constructed in one process (storage-server module and `ProvideUnifiedStorageClient`'s default local-SQL path both call sql.NewResourceServer with search enabled). HOW: in `bleveBackend.BuildIndex`, fall back to `bleve.Open(dir)` when `bleve.New` returns `bleve.ErrorIndexPathExists` (or remove the stale dir before rebuilding); alternatively, make Init failures at construction non-fatal/retryable instead of aborting `NewResourceServer`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Newly added init-time TotalDocs() call iterates the bleve cache map without its mutex while the just-started watch-event goroutine can concurrently write a new index into it, crashing the process with a fatal concurrent-map-access error.
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: the newly added `s.search.TotalDocs()` call (search.go:216) executes `bleveBackend.TotalDocs` (bleve.go:144-154), which range-iterates the shared `b.cache` map without acquiring `cacheMu`, and it runs right after the watch-event goroutine has been started at search.go:207-213. WHY: any WrittenEvent arriving in that window for a resource kind that init skipped (count <= IndexMinCount, default 1 — init only builds stats with count > 1) or a brand-new kind drives handleEvent -> getOrCreateIndex -> BuildIndex -> `b.cache[key] = idx` (bleve.go:137-139) while TotalDocs is mid-iteration; concurrent map iteration and map write is an unrecoverable Go runtime fatal error that crashes the entire Grafana process. The same unlocked read already exists via the prometheus collector (bleve_index_metrics.go:96), so the root flaw is pre-existing, but this PR adds a call site that by construction races with the just-started event goroutine during startup. HOW: acquire `b.cacheMu.RLock()` (with defer RUnlock) at the top of `bleveBackend.TotalDocs()`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The added t.Skip for dbType == "postgres" neutralises the only integration test that boots the storage-server target and asserts the instrumentation server serves http://localhost:3001/metrics. With this skip, when CI runs with GRAFANA_TEST_DB=postgres the test exits at line 37 before InitializeModuleServer is ever called, so the suite stays green even if the postgres storage-server target fails to start or /metrics never serves — the behaviour the test is named after. The skip was added in the same PR that changes NewResourceServer to call s.Init(ctx) synchronously (pkg/storage/unified/resource/server.go:258), which now runs the full search-index build (searchSupport.init -> GetResourceStats SQL) at construction; the skip message itself says "test not working with postgres in Drone", which strongly suggests this PR's eager-Init change broke the postgres path and the skip is hiding that regression rather than the test being fixed. Either fix the test (or the underlying postgres failure) so it actually runs, or assert/document the concrete failure mode; leaving it skipped means a broken postgres behaviour cannot be caught by any test. The postgres branch of addStorageServerToConfig (lines 75-79) is also now unreachable dead test code.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: NewResourceServer now synchronously runs Init (full search index build) and fails construction on init errors, a contract change its callers were not updated for.
suggestions.suggestionContent: NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) synchronously, changing the constructor's behavior contract: previously it returned immediately (old code returned at what is now line 264 without initializing), and Init was invoked separately — with errors logged inside once.Do (server.go:313-315) rather than failing construction. Now the constructor blocks for the entire search index build (s.search.init builds every tenant/resource index, which can take minutes on large instances) and returns an error on any init failure (line 261). Consumers of NewResourceServer were not updated for this: a transient index-build error that previously degraded search now prevents the server (and Grafana startup) from being constructed at all. Either keep the constructor non-fatal (log and continue, letting search fail per-request as before) or update every construction site to expect a blocking, fallible constructor.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: TotalDocs reads b.cache without cacheMu while BuildIndex writes it under the lock, and the newly added call in searchSupport.init can race with the just-started watch-event goroutine's BuildIndex, risking a fatal concurrent map read/write panic.
suggestions.suggestionContent: BuildIndex (changed in this PR) now writes b.cache under cacheMu (bleve.go:137-139), but TotalDocs (bleve.go:144-154) — newly called in production from searchSupport.init at resource/search.go:216 — ranges over b.cache without acquiring cacheMu. The watch-event goroutine started at resource/search.go:207-213 can concurrently reach BuildIndex via handleEvent → getOrCreateIndex → build for any key not indexed during init (count ≤ initMinSize or a new resource type), so the unlocked map read can overlap the locked map write and trigger a fatal "concurrent map read and map write" panic, crashing the process during startup. Guard the read with the same mutex the writer uses: take b.cacheMu.Lock() (defer Unlock) at the top of TotalDocs so the two sites agree on the cache's synchronization contract.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Reordering watcher startup after the search index build creates a window where writes during startup are published to the broadcaster before the search subscriber exists and are therefore never indexed.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The reorder moves initWatcher() (server.go:308-311) after s.search.init(ctx) (server.go:303-306). Writes that occur during the synchronous index build go through server.Write -> s.broadcaster.Publish, but the search event handler (searchSupport.handleEvent) only subscribes when initWatcher runs — so events published during the build window are never indexed, leaving search results permanently stale for those writes. The previous ordering (watcher first) covered this window. Either restore watcher-first ordering with buffering for indexes not yet built, or after the build verify each index's RV against backend stats and rebuild/apply missed events.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Delete and Pause/Resume actions never render in the new ruler-less alert list view because AlertRuleMenu still gates them on rulerRule.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Federated Mimir rule groups are no longer treated as immutable, so the Edit button now appears for read-only federated rules in the existing rules table.
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: useAllAlertRuleAbilities previously computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` to treat federated rule groups as immutable, but the new implementation (useAbilities.ts:222-229) delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities which hardcodes `isFederated = false` (useAbilities.ts:243-245, "TODO: Add support for federated rules"), dropping the check. suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The new comment in useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities says prom rules are 'always supported (no loading state)' while the code gates support on a loading flag.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The comment added at useAbilities.ts:308 — 'GrafanaPromRuleDTO rules are always supported (no loading state for ruler availability)' — contradicts the very next line: `const MaybeSupported = loading ? NotSupported : AlwaysSupported;`. suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities leaves a stray, meaningless `// duplicate` marker on the useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable call.

It does not correspond to anything in the code: useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable is defined once and nothing on this line duplicates anything. suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Deprecated useAllAlertRuleAbilities now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities which hardcodes isFederated = false, so read-only Mimir federated rule groups lose their immutability gating and Edit/Delete/Pause get offered.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: GrafanaGroupLoader's JSDoc still says it loads from Prometheus and Ruler endpoints although this PR removed the ruler API query.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The PR removed the ruler API query (useGetGrafanaRulerGroupQuery) and the matchRules logic from GrafanaGroupLoader — it now fetches only via useGetGrafanaGroupsQuery — but left the component's documentation describing the old behaviour. Since token-type shortcuts are always 'rt'/'lt' (index 3 is always 't'), substring(3,5) can never equal any two-letter grant shortcut, so the guard is unreachable dead code and the matcher accepts tokens of ANY grant type — every expectCodeToToken/expectRefresh/expectDeviceToken/expectAuthReqIdToToken TOKEN_ID grant assertion added by this PR silently passes regardless of grant. suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: the common-prefix (`start`) / common-suffix (`end`) trimming used to build the "Illegal HTML in key ..." message can overlap and throw: when the whole `value` is a prefix of `sanitized` (e.g. `Some text>` → OWASP sanitizer auto-closes to `Some text>`) and the last characters match, `start == value.length()` while `end >= 1`, so `value.substring(start, value.length() - end)` is invoked with begin > end. WHY: `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException` propagates out of `verify()` as a raw RuntimeException and fails the mojo build with a stack trace instead of the intended validation message — precisely on the path that already detected a bad translation. HOW: clamp before slicing, e.g. stop the suffix loop at `end < value.length() - start` (and symmetrically for sanitized), or guard `if (value.length() - end >= start && sanitized.length() - end >= start)` around the `messages.add(...)` call.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The common-prefix/common-suffix trimming in the 'Illegal HTML' diagnostic can overlap, making substring(start, len-end) receive begin > end and throw StringIndexOutOfBoundsException, crashing the verifier on exactly the malformed translations it is meant to report.

Clamp the end indices (e.g. Math.max(start, length - end)) before calling substring.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: ANCHOR_PATTERN `</?a[^>]*>` matches every tag whose name starts with 'a' (<abbr>, <address>, <audio>, ...), so such tags are silently stripped before the whitelist check, producing false negatives in the HTML-safety verifier.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The anchor pattern has no boundary after the element name: `</?a[^>]*>` also matches `<abbr>`, `<address>`, `<audio>`, `<article>`, etc. Because santizeAnchors() deletes from `value` any tag that appears identically in the English string before the policy check runs, such non-anchor tags silently bypass the br/p/strong/b whitelist — the verifier reports nothing where it should report 'Illegal HTML'. Require the tag name to end after the 'a', e.g. `</?a(?:\s[^>]*)?>`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Client deletion fails with UnsupportedOperationException when both FGAP V1 and V2 features are enabled
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled (ClientPermissionsV2.java:192-195) throws UnsupportedOperationException, but AdminPermissions.registerListener (AdminPermissions.java:77-91, modified in this PR) calls management(session, realm).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false) on every ClientModel.ClientRemovedEvent, guarded only by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag, while AdminPermissions.management() (AdminPermissions.java:66-71) selects MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled. WHY: with both features enabled at once (a valid combination — Profile.java:58 declares ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 as a separate experimental feature depending only on Feature.AUTHORIZATION), every client removal publishes the event (JpaRealmProvider.java:1006) and DefaultKeycloakSessionFactory.publish (DefaultKeycloakSessionFactory.java:86-90) iterates listeners without any try/catch, so the UnsupportedOperationException propagates and aborts the DELETE /admin/realms/{realm}/clients/{id} transaction — client deletion becomes impossible. Secondary: in V2-only mode the guard silently skips cleanup, leaving orphaned per-client resources/permissions for deleted clients. HOW: also skip the listener when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled (or make ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled(client, false) a no-op/delete-the-resource implementation instead of throwing).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: getClientsWithPermission can return the non-client-ID string "Clients" (and misses per-client resources), causing an NPE in its only caller
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: getClientsWithPermission (ClientPermissionsV2.java:138-144) enumerates resources with resourceStore.findByType(server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and adds resource.getName() to the returned set, but per-client resources created by AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource (AdminPermissionsSchema.java:103-111) never have a `type` attribute set (only create(server, name, owner) + updateScopes), so per-client grants are not matched by the type query; meanwhile the schema-level "Clients" type resource does match the query, so when an all-clients scope permission grants the requested scope the literal string "Clients" — not a client UUID — is added to the result. WHY: the only production caller, AvailableRoleMappingResource.getRoleIdsWithPermissions (rest/admin-ui-ext/.../AvailableRoleMappingResource.java:229-230), dereferences every entry via realm.getClientById(cid).getRolesStream(), so the bogus "Clients" entry (or entries for deleted clients, since the V2 listener no longer cleans up resources on client removal) causes a NullPointerException/500 on the admin console available-role-mapping endpoints; and for admins holding only per-client map-roles permissions the returned set is silently empty, so available client roles are never listed. This breaks the V1 contract (ClientPermissions.java:667-687) where the method returns real client IDs (type "Client" + "client.resource." prefix stripping). HOW: skip the type resource in the findByType consumer (exclude the resource whose name equals CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and ensure per-client resources are created with type=CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE (e.g. resource.setType(...) in getOrCreateResource) so the enumeration only yields valid client IDs.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Realm-wide canView() ignores all-clients manage permission, causing 403s for manage-all admins
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: the realm-wide canView() override (ClientPermissionsV2.java:86-88) accepts only the all-clients `view` scope, so a fine-grained admin granted only all-clients `manage` fails every realm-wide view check. WHY: requireList()/requireListClientScopes()/requireViewClientScopes() funnel through canView() — e.g. GET /admin/realms/{realm}/clients throws 403 at ClientsResource.java:120 (auth.clients().requireList()), and client-scope listing throws 403 via canViewClientScopes() → canView() — even though the same admin can create, update and delete every client because canManage() (line 73) and canManageClientScopes() (line 109) do honor the manage scope. PermissionClientTest.testManageAllClients only passes because myadmin additionally holds the QUERY_USERS role (RealmAdminPermissionsConfig.java:34). This is inconsistent with the sibling UserPermissionsV2.canView (UserPermissionsV2.java:52) which treats manage as implying view by passing both VIEW and MANAGE scopes, and with this class's own canView(ClientScopeModel) (line 121) which checks VIEW || MANAGE. HOW: include the manage scope, e.g. `return canViewClientDefault() || hasPermission(AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW) || hasPermission(AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE);` (or delegate to canManageClientScopes()).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Possible null resource passed to findByResource when the "Clients" type resource does not exist
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: hasPermission(ClientModel, String) (ClientPermissionsV2.java:215-221) assigns the result of AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(...) and passes it unchecked into policyStore.findByResource(server, resource), but getResourceTypeResource only performs findByName and returns null when the "Clients" type resource does not exist (AdminPermissionsSchema.java:116-134 — it never creates). WHY: any realm whose admin-permissions resource server was initialized before this PR added the Clients type is missing that resource — SCHEMA.init only runs at realm creation (RealmManager.java:572), and the adminPermissionsClient import path (RealmManager.java:567-570) creates the resource server while skipping SCHEMA.init entirely — so every per-client check (canManage/canView/canConfigure/canMapRoles on a client that has no per-client resource) dereferences the null resource inside findByResource and throws, turning admin client operations into 500s. The sibling hasPermission(String) overload in the same file (ClientPermissionsV2.java:244-247) does null-check, so the asymmetry looks unintended. HOW: after line 217 add `if (resource == null) return false;` mirroring lines 245-247.

suggestions.label: bug

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: getClientsWithPermission assumes every resource of type Clients is named by a client ID, so the all-clients sentinel resource pollutes the returned set and all-clients grants yield no real client IDs.
suggestions.suggestionContent: getClientsWithPermission iterates every resource of type "Clients" and adds resource.getName() to a set documented/used as client IDs. The schema also maintains a type-level "all-clients" resource named "Clients" (the same object hasPermission(String) at line 244 looks up via findByName(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...)), and it carries the same resource type, so findByType returns it. When an all-clients scope permission grants the scope, hasGrantedPermission evaluates true for that sentinel resource and the literal string "Clients" is added to the set, while none of the real client IDs covered by the all-clients grant are. Callers that filter clients via set.contains(client.getId()) will get an empty/wrong list for admins who hold all-clients permissions — the fix is to skip the type-level resource by name (and decide with the callers how an all-clients grant should be signalled, since excluding it silently still leaves the "all clients" case unrepresented in the set).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Client deletion under the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ feature invokes ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled, which throws UnsupportedOperationException, breaking the cleanup listener in AdminPermissions.
suggestions.suggestionContent: ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled (lines 192-195) throws UnsupportedOperationException, but it is invoked unconditionally by the ProviderEventListener registered in AdminPermissions.java:89-91 (this PR's hunk) on every ClientModel.ClientRemovedEvent, gated on Profile.isFeatureEnabled(ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ) — i.e. exactly when MgmtPermissionsV2 (MgmtPermissionsV2.java:63-68, also this PR) is active and clients() returns ClientPermissionsV2. So in any feature-enabled realm, deleting a client (as PermissionClientTest.testManageAllClients itself does) hits the throwing implementation: the exception surfaces in the removal event (breaking/logging on every client delete), and the cleanup it was meant to perform — deleting the per-client "Clients" authorization resource created via AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource — never happens, orphaning resources for every deleted client. setPermissionsEnabled should be a no-op when disabling in V2 (or implement V2 resource cleanup), or the AdminPermissions listener must be adjusted for the V2 path; note the sibling paths (roles(), groups()) still resolve to V1 implementations and do not throw — only the clients() path was rewired by this PR.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Password page now discloses passkey-credential configuration (and potentially credential IDs) for an arbitrary typed username to unauthenticated visitors.
suggestions.suggestionContent: In the identity-first (username form -> PasswordForm) login flow, context.getUser() is set from the username the visitor typed, with no credential verified yet. The newly added webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) in PasswordForm.render (and the relaxed isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser()) guard in UsernamePasswordForm.challenge, lines 137-140) now embeds per-user WebAuthn data into that unauthenticated response. The mere presence of the webauthn form discloses to an anonymous visitor that the typed username belongs to an existing account with passkey credentials configured (and where the `authenticators` attribute is populated, the new authn_select block in themes/src/main/resources/theme/base/login/passkeys.ftl renders the account's passkey credentialIds into the page source). Pre-PR, the password page response was uniform regardless of the typed username (webauthn data was only filled when the user was not yet selected). Consider gating the per-user passkey data on the user already being authenticated (e.g., re-authentication, where USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH indicates the session owner) rather than on any user merely present in the authentication context, or document/accept the enumeration trade-off explicitly for the identity-first flow.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The new re-auth error-path assertions verify a message produced independently of the refactored AuthenticatorUtils.setupReauthenticationInUsernamePasswordFormError, so deleting that method leaves all PR tests green.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The wrong-password-during-re-auth assertions in this PR do not verify the behaviour this PR changed. "Invalid password." is produced by getDefaultChallengeMessage() (AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator lines 249-255, driven by the USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH auth note) plus the hardcoded FIELD_PASSWORD in badPasswordHandler line 224 — none of it depends on AuthenticatorUtils.setupReauthenticationInUsernamePasswordFormError (the code the PR moved at AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator.java:222). Consequently, if that util method were deleted or stopped setting USERNAME_HIDDEN/REGISTRATION_DISABLED (e.g. the username input becomes editable and the registration link reappears on the re-auth error form), every test in this PR would still pass, and the PR's new call site in WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator.errorChallenge (passkey error during re-auth) is not exercised by any test at all. Strengthen the re-auth error assertions to check the actual form attributes: after the failed password in webauthnLoginWithExternalKey_reauthenticationWithPasswordOrPasskey (and in PasskeysUsernameFormTest.passwordLogin_reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey), assert that the username input is not present / not editable (e.g. loginPage.isUsernameInputPresent() is false, or the attempted username renders as static text) and the registration link is absent; and add a test that fails/cancels the conditional passkey during prompt=login re-authentication to cover the new errorChallenge path.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Passkey form is now populated with the typed user's credential IDs on pages reachable with only a username, disclosing account existence/credential metadata to unauthenticated requesters.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The new isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() guard drops the previous 'user is not already selected' condition (old code: context.getUser() == null), so during a normal (non re-authentication) login the passkey form is now filled with the typed user's WebAuthn credential IDs and authenticator labels and served to a requester who has not presented any credential. Anyone who knows a username (a public identifier) can, by merely entering it, learn that the account exists and has passkeys and obtain its credential IDs/labels (passkeys.ftl renders the 'authenticators' block with credentialId inputs), also weakening the generic 'invalid username or password' error by conditionally rendering the webauthn form. Consider only filling the per-user passkey data when the requester is already authenticated as that user (i.e., when the USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH auth note is set, as in re-authentication), and for unauthenticated sessions keep the generic discoverable-credential conditional UI without the per-user authenticator/credentialId list.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Re-auth tests assert a LOGIN event without clearing the event list first, so the assertion can be satisfied by the earlier, identical first-login event.
suggestions.suggestionContent: In webauthnLoginWithDiscoverableKey_reauthentication (and the identical pattern in PasskeysOrganizationAuthenticationTest.webauthnLoginWithDiscoverableKey_reauthentication), the final events.expectLogin()...assertEvent() after the prompt=login re-authentication runs without an events.clear() since the first login, and the expected details (user, CREDENTIAL_TYPE=TYPE_PASSWORDLESS, USER_VERIFICATION_CHECKED=true) are identical to the first login event already asserted earlier in the same test. The assertion can therefore be satisfied by the stale first-login event and does not actually verify that the re-authentication produced a LOGIN event with the passwordless credential details — the event-detail part of the test's claim would still pass if broken. Add events.clear() right before the re-authentication (after the first assertEvent), matching what webauthnLoginWithExternalKey_reauthenticationWithPasswordOrPasskey in the same PR correctly does before its final assertions.

suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Wrapped original vs raw updated predicate asymmetry can skip login-cache invalidation, leaving disabled IDPs served from the getForLogin cache when an organization is disabled.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Error-event timestamps read verbatim from nodestore are ISO strings for real ingested events, so comparing them against numeric replay-segment breadcrumb timestamps raises TypeError and 500s the summarize-breadcrumbs endpoint.

The PR's test only survives because `store_event` is handed a raw float that bypasses normalization. Normalize the value explicitly (parse ISO strings to a unix float, wrapped in try/except with a numeric fallback) before putting it into `ErrorEvent`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: join() breaks out of the process loop once the deadline passes, leaving remaining flusher processes unjoined and un-terminated.
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: `join()` uses `break` when the deadline has expired, so once the timeout budget is spent, all flusher processes after the current iteration index are never `terminate()`d (and never waited on). WHY: `self.next_step.join(timeout)` runs before the loop and can consume the entire timeout, making `remaining_time <= 0` true on the *first* iteration — then NO process is terminated at all; and for any hung process (exactly the scenario join-with-timeout exists for) the process never exits on its own because it never rechecks `stopped`. Since `close()` deliberately does not stop flusher processes and the SpanFlusher is discarded after each rebalance (`create_with_partitions` builds a new one), un-terminated hung processes leak permanently and keep flushing shards that may have been reassigned to another consumer — resource leak plus duplicate segment production. HOW: replace `break` with `continue` so each remaining process still falls through to `process.terminate()` (and consider joining with the remaining time).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Per-process buffers make spans.buffer.max-flush-segments a per-process budget and delay the any_shard_at_limit backpressure trigger by ~P×.
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: Each flusher process now gets its own `SpansBuffer` covering only its shard subset, but `SpansBuffer.flush_segments` (buffer.py:382-384) computes `max_segments_per_shard = ceil(spans.buffer.max-flush-segments / len(assigned_shards))` — so the divisor changed from the total shard count to the per-process subset size. WHY: with one process per shard (the PR's stated goal), each process flushes up to the full `max-flush-segments` budget per cycle (total flush volume = P × option value) and, more importantly, `any_shard_at_limit` backpressure only fires when a single shard's queue is ~P× deeper than before — so the `MessageRejected` guard that pauses ingestion to protect Redis memory engages ~P× later, letting Redis queues grow ~P× deeper before the consumer pauses. The option silently changes meaning from "total segments per flush cycle" to "total segments per flush cycle per process". HOW: if the backpressure threshold must keep its old absolute meaning, derive the per-shard limit from the total assigned-shard count (pass it into the per-process buffer) or rescale `spans.buffer.max-flush-segments` when `--flusher-processes > 1`; at minimum document that the option is now per-process.

suggestions.label: performance
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: submit() now performs one duplicate cluster-wide Redis memory scan per flusher buffer, all against the same Redis cluster.
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: When `spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage` is enabled, `submit()` now calls `buffer.get_memory_info()` once per flusher buffer, but every buffer's client points at the same fixed Redis cluster (`get_redis_client()` → `redis.redis_cluster.get_binary(settings.SENTRY_SPAN_BUFFER_CLUSTER)`), so these are P identical duplicate cluster-wide memory scans (iter_cluster_memory_usage INFO round trips across cluster nodes) per submitted batch. WHY: old code did one scan per submit; with P flusher processes this becomes P redundant scans per batch, linear in process count, on the consumer's submit path. HOW: since the result is identical for all buffers, call `get_memory_info()` once on any single buffer (e.g. `next(iter(self.buffers.values()))` or the original full-shard buffer) instead of extending a list per buffer.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: wait_produce timer uses tag key "shards" while sibling flusher metrics use "shard", breaking shard-grouped aggregation.
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: The `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` timer is tagged with key `"shards"` while every other metric in the same loop uses `"shard"` (flusher.py:185, 195, and flusher_unhealthy at line 244). WHY: the same shard-dimension is emitted under two different tag keys, so dashboards/alerts grouping flusher metrics by `shard` silently miss this timer and the shard breakdown for produce-wait latency appears untagged/duplicated. HOW: change `tags={"shards": shard_tag}` to `tags={"shard": shard_tag}`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Truthiness check `max_processes or len(...)` treats an explicit 0 as "auto" (max fan-out) and lets negatives create zero flusher processes, causing silent Redis pile-up with no health detection.
suggestions.suggestionContent: `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` conflates an explicit falsy 0 with the None sentinel, and lets negatives through to `min()`. Traced: the CLI option `--flusher-processes` (consumers/__init__.py) is `type=int` with no bounds. Passing 0 (falsy) silently escalates to one process per shard — the maximum — even though the help text says "Defaults to 1" and the signature reserves None for the auto behavior; a user configuring 0 to stay on the previous single-process behavior gets the opposite. Passing any negative value (truthy) survives the `or`, so `num_processes = min(-1, len(shards)) = -1`, `range(-1)` is empty, and zero flusher processes are created: `self.buffers` is empty so `record_stored_segments()` is never called, `_ensure_processes_alive()` iterates an empty dict so no hang/crash detection or restart ever fires, and no process ever flushes Redis — segments accumulate indefinitely while the consumer reports healthy and backpressure can never trigger (its flags are only set inside a flusher process's main loop). Fix by distinguishing None from 0 explicitly and clamping: `self.max_processes = len(buffer.assigned_shards) if max_processes is None else max(1, max_processes)`, or add `type=click.IntRange(min=1)` to the click option.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: test_basic's added time.sleep(0.1) is neutralized by the test's own time.sleep monkeypatch, so the flusher-thread wait it promises never happens and the assertion races the background thread.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The `time.sleep(0.1)` added at line 62 is a no-op: line 15 monkeypatches "time.sleep" to `lambda _: None` module-wide, so this call returns instantly and the "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change" wait never happens. The flusher thread only produces during a `while not stopped.value` loop iteration (flusher.py:166-169) that reads current_drift after it was set to 9000, and step.join() sets stopped=True (flusher.py:331) immediately afterwards; the thread can observe stopped before the drift, exit without producing, and leave `messages` empty so `(msg,) = messages` fails spuriously. The test currently passes only because step.poll()'s Redis calls incidentally release the GIL for the spinning thread. Capture the real sleep before patching and wait on a condition (messages non-empty) with a deadline instead of a fixed — and silently removed — sleep.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Newly added shard tags use key "shard" on two metrics but "shards" on the sibling wait_produce timer, fragmenting the dimension and breaking shard-grouped queries.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The three metrics newly tagged in this PR use two different tag keys for the same dimension: `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` (line 185) and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` (line 195) emit tags={"shard": shard_tag}, while the sibling `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` (line 199) emits tags={"shards": shard_tag}. (Related consistency note: `_ensure_processes_alive` emits `flusher_unhealthy` with singular per-shard ids under the same `shard` key while main() uses comma-joined shard_tag — worth unifying the value format too.)

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: `_create_process_for_shard` is added by this PR but never called — dead leftover that would also leak the old process if ever used.
suggestions.suggestionContent: `_create_process_for_shard` (lines 127-132) is newly added by this PR but has no caller anywhere: `_create_processes` calls `_create_process_for_shards` (line 84) and the restart path in `_ensure_processes_alive` also calls `_create_process_for_shards` directly (line 259). Worse, if it were ever wired up it would restart a process's shards without killing the old (possibly hung) process, since it never kills `self.processes[process_index]` before overwriting it — leaking the old process and its shared mp.Value state. Remove the dead method, or route restarts through it and kill the old process first.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The `time.sleep(0.1)` added to let flusher threads catch up is a no-op because `time.sleep` is monkeypatched to a lambda at the top of the same test.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The added `time.sleep(0.1)` (line 62), commented "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change", never actually waits: line 15 of the same test monkeypatches `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None` globally, so this call returns instantly and provides no synchronization before `step.join()` sets the shared `stopped` flag. The line only misleads readers into thinking the race with join() is handled. Either wait using a mechanism that isn't patched (e.g. save `real_sleep = time.sleep` before monkeypatching and call that, or poll for the expected message with a timeout), or drop the dead line if the busy-spinning flusher loop (whose own `time.sleep(1)` is also patched) already makes the test deterministic.

suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is always False for the spawn-context SpawnProcess instances SpanFlusher creates, so the restart path never kills a hung process before spawning its replacement.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The new guard `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process): process.kill()` in `_ensure_processes_alive` never fires, because SpanFlusher creates its processes with `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process` (flusher.py:53, 105), which produces `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess` instances. `SpawnProcess` is a sibling of `multiprocessing.Process` (both subclass `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`), so the isinstance check is False for every process this class manages — and also for the test-mode `threading.Thread`. The old code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally, which correctly killed a hung spawn process before respawning; now `kill()` is dead code. Consequence: when a flusher process hangs (the `cause == "hang"` path — the process is still alive), `_create_process_for_shards` starts a replacement without stopping the hung one, so two processes flush the same shards concurrently (duplicate Kafka production races), the hung process leaks a Kafka producer and stays alive as a zombie, and each subsequent hang adds another. Fix by checking the concrete type the class actually creates (note the file's own annotation already uses `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`), e.g. `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess): process.kill()`, or invert it with `if not isinstance(process, threading.Thread): process.kill()`. The same wrong isinstance also gates `process.terminate()` in `join()` (flusher.py:346-347), making that shutdown safety net a no-op too — fix both.

suggestions.suggestionContent: The constructor no longer guarantees that at least one flusher process exists. `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` handles None/0, but a negative `--flusher-processes` value (click's `type=int` accepts it) is truthy, so `num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(shards))` goes negative and `range(self.num_processes)` is empty: zero processes are created, and `self.processes`, `self.buffers` and `self.process_backpressure_since` are all empty. The consumer then keeps accepting and writing spans to Redis while nothing ever flushes (`_ensure_processes_alive` iterates an empty dict, and the backpressure/memory checks never trigger because there are no values to read), i.e. a silent unbounded backlog — whereas before this change the flusher always ran exactly one process. Clamp the value, e.g. `self.max_processes = max(1, max_processes) if max_processes else len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, or validate the click option with a positive-int range.

The previous version was concrete (evaluate() returned []) and degraded gracefully. Either implement the three abstract methods for metric alerts, or leave MetricAlertFire.detector_handler unset (None) until the handler is actually ready so process_detectors skips it instead of crashing.

suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Test helper build_mock_occurrence_and_event accepts a `value` parameter it never uses, and the expected occurrences are built with value 6 while the actual evaluated values are 10, 100, and 8, so the tests never verify the value passed to the new build_occurrence_and_event_data hook.
suggestions.suggestionContent: `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` declares `value: int` but never uses it in the occurrence or event_data it builds. Because the parameter is dead, the expected results constructed in test_state_results_multi_group (value 6 for "group_2" whose actual packet value is 10), test_results_on_change (6 vs actual 100), and test_dedupe (6 vs actual 8) all pass while disagreeing with the real evaluated values. As a result, the new abstract hook `StatefulDetectorHandler.build_occurrence_and_event_data(group_key, value, new_status)` is not actually tested to receive the correct per-group value — a regression in the handler that passed the wrong value to the hook would go unnoticed. Either incorporate `value` into the mock (e.g., in `subtitle` or `evidence_data`) so mismatches surface, or at minimum pass the true evaluated values at the expected-construction call sites.

suggestions.suggestionContent: The docstring of `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` still reads "Evaluates a given data packet and returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`.", but this PR changed both `evaluate` overrides (and the abstract `DetectorHandler.evaluate` at lines 125-129) to return `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`, and `process_detectors` (line 49) was updated to iterate `.values()`. The docstring now describes a return shape the function no longer produces — a caller reading it will treat the result as a list. Update the docstring to say it returns a dict of results keyed by group key.

suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: get_monitor_environment_context builds a transformed config copy but returns the raw monitor.config, silently dropping the schedule_type display conversion from the produced issue event context.
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: `get_monitor_environment_context` computes `config = monitor_environment.monitor.config.copy()` and replaces `config["schedule_type"]` with `monitor.get_schedule_type_display()` (incident_occurrence.py:160-162), but the returned dict at line 168 embeds `monitor_environment.monitor.config` — the original, untransformed config — so the transformed `config` local is dead code. WHY: the monitor context embedded in the issue-platform occurrence payload (`event_data["contexts"]["monitor"]`, produced to Kafka at incident_occurrence.py:109) carries the raw integer `schedule_type` (config stores an integer per models.py:55; `get_schedule_type_display()` at models.py:343-344 returns `ScheduleType.get_name(...)`), so the intended human-readable schedule type never reaches the event and the copy/mutation at lines 160-162 has no effect. This bug was carried over verbatim from the old `mark_failed.py`, but this PR is the split-out that moves this function into its own module, making now the natural point to fix it. HOW: return `"config": config` instead of `"config": monitor_environment.monitor.config` in the dict at line 168.
